utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-03-67-R77.3, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Seselj, would you confirm that the system is working and that you can hear me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you in the Serbian language, but it seems that you have not heard me. As far as I'm concerned, the system is operational.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. I now have it. I didn't have translation immediately on my channel 4, but I have it now. Thank you. Do I confirm you still represent yourself in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I told you at the initial appearance and at the first Status Conference that I will continue representing myself until the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I haven't forgotten that, but for the record, it's something that I will ask on each occasion so that the record is clear on this point. And may we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm Bruce MacFarlane, the amicus curiae Prosecutor appointed in these proceedings, and to my right is Lori Ann Wanlin, who is with me this afternoon and throughout these proceedings, and is also a member of a Canadian Bar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, today is another Status Conference as mandated by the Rules. The last Status Conference in this case was held on the 3rd of September of this year, and the purpose of these Status Conferences, according to the Rules, are, and I am repeating what I would have said on the last occasion, to organise exchanges between the parties so that the path to the trial is expedited and to review the status of the accused's case and to allow the accused to raise any issues which are related thereto, and also to raise any matter related to his -- the circumstances of his confinement or his -- his physical condition. Now, there are a number of motions which were pending at the -- which were pending the motion for disqualification of Judges Kwon and Parker which had been filed by the accused on the 27th of April, and a specially appointed Chamber dismissed the motions on the 19th of November, 2010. Since then the Chamber has issued decisions on all pending motions save one, and could we go into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane, on the 10th of December, that's Friday last, the Chamber issued a decision on the accused's requests for access to additional documents. Could you confirm that once the material indicated therein is provided to the accused your disclosure obligations pursuant to Rule 66(A) have been met?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I can confirm that they will be met upon the service of the material referred to in that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Do you have any further comments to make on --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Not on the question of disclosure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And again for the record, I would remind the amicus Prosecutor that -- of the ongoing obligation pursuant to Rule 66 to disclose to the accused any material which in his actual knowledge, that is the Prosecutor's actual knowledge, may suggest innocence or mitigate the guilt of the accused or affect the credibility of the Prosecution's evidence. Mr. MacFarlane, are there any other matters on -- you said you have nothing further on disclosure. Mr. Seselj, do you have anything further -- any further representations to make to the Chamber on this question of disclosure?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm prepared to submit my motion under Rule 65 ter as early as tomorrow. I would like to disclose to the opposing side the statements of ten witnesses I intend to call, and those are the preliminary statements based on which I will conduct the examination-in-chief, and in addition to that, I would also submit photocopies of various interviews given by these witnesses to the newspapers. The Prosecution has that in principle, but in order to avoid duplication of work, meaning the translation, the translation services of the Tribunal should check whether any of those interviews and statements had already been translated so as not to do it twice. It is my intention to speed up the proceedings, not to slow them down. These ten witnesses would require one hour each in examination-in-chief. I could have disclosed that this morning, because my wife brought it in with her today. However, I received that quite late, just before coming here to the Tribunal, so I didn't have the time to do it today. I propose to do it tomorrow or the day after tomorrow so that all of these statements can be translated so that they can be used in January. So I'm quite ahead of the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor hasn't disclosed anything under Rule 65 ter. I guess he doesn't have anything. He still hasn't disclosed any of the material that according to your order he was supposed to disclose pursuant to your order of 10th of December. Anyway, I'm prepared to start the proceedings in the early part of January. I'm done as far as the disclosure is concerned. I have some other matters to raise. Would you like me to do it right away?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I'd hear whether Mr. MacFarlane has any further to say on this matter of disclosure and then we will come back to you on the other matters. Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In terms of the ten pages that are in issue and were the subject of the order of the Chamber, on conferring with the Registry, it's my understanding that the Registry will be arranging to have that provided to the accused, and that will be done very shortly. I have no further comments on -- on disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have some other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] May I have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. The Registry confirmed that those 11 pages were provided to you yesterday and you signed as having received them. Yes, Mr. Seselj, your other matters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These 11 pages mean nothing for my defence, and it is clear to anybody who takes a look at them. What is important for my defence, however, has not been disclosed to me. Pursuant to your order of 10th December, it is not clear whether that needs to be disclosed to me. It says in that order that you partially granted my motion, but it doesn't spell out what has been denied, and I think that it pertains to the documents that I enumerated at the last Status Conference and the one before that in which one can see why the Trial Chamber refused to initiate contempt proceedings against me two years ago. The facts are the same as they are now. The reasoning of the Trial Chamber at that time is important for me, for my defence, because the Trial Chamber then had the two Judges that are in the current Trial Chamber as well, and two years ago they did not want to initiate these proceedings and now they decided otherwise. Without that material, my defence would not be complete. I will, nevertheless, proceed with my defence, but I will keep reiterating that I did not receive the material I requested, and that will be the first ground in the appeal against the judgement rendered in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So noted. What are the other matters you wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Technical issues that need to be resolved. I think that you, Mr. Hall, as a Pre-Trial Judge, should raise this with the Registry. Since I will be calling ten witnesses in my defence case, I need assistance of my legal assistant, Dejan Mirovic, and Case Manager Nemanja Sarovic. I need the two of them to be here in The Hague the entire time. I need them to have a hotel, per diem allowance, transportation, and so on. In addition to that, I need to see each of the witnesses I intend to call. I need to proof them, and I need to see them in the detention unit. As you know, witnesses are proofed in this Tribunal. Very few witnesses come to testify without being proofed. As a result, I would like to proof my witnesses, and all of this is aimed towards splintering into smithereens this order in lieu of indictment against me. In this main case against me, the Trial Chamber was just about to resolve the issue of funding my defence case. They had a discussion with the Registry. I'm not asking for any fees to be paid out in this particular case. I just ask that the costs be covered for my legal assistants as well as for the witnesses who are about to come to testify in this case. And as is normal in other cases, all witnesses should be entitled to have one person accompany them when they travel to The Hague, and I will be ready to start calling these witnesses in early January. There is no need for me to wait for Mr. MacFarlane's pre-trial brief. I also don't need to see his 65 ter list with documents he intends to tender. Those mostly boil down to photocopies of my books and material from previous cases about protective measures for these witnesses. I intend to call witnesses who will confirm in this courtroom that it was them who disclosed their identity. It wasn't me. I disclosed the statements they provided for my defence. I did not disclose the statements they provided earlier to the OTP when the OTP intended to call them as witnesses. These are two very different things. Each of these witnesses came out and publicly stated, "I was asked to come and testify. The OTP wanted to force me to testify for them. They forced me to sign a false statement." Those are the kind of things that they will say. We will discuss these matters here in the courtroom, and this is what my defence is based upon. It is important for me to have a Legal Assistant and Case Manager here so that there are no hindrances in my defence preparations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the Registry would be aware of the request which you are now making, and I fully expect that there is or there are well-established procedures for dealing with the type of assistance which you have indicated that you require. Are there any other matters which you wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. The -- Mr. MacFarlane, the last comment that the accused has made is a useful link to the question of -- I would ask of you, whether you intend to call any witnesses in the course of the trial, and the context in which that is being asked is with a view to plotting out the progress of this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. At present, I do not anticipate any -- calling any viva voce evidence through witnesses. The case for the Prosecution will consist of a paper trail, and as a result of that, I expect that the case for the Prosecution can be presented with dispatch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, the -- we now know that the accused intends to call, he says, ten witnesses, and the Trial Chamber, having this information, will inform the parties as to a projected trial date. Are there any other matters which either side wishes to raise at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I've few matters, if I might, at this stage, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: In terms of the readiness for the case to proceed, I simply wish to advise the Chamber that the Prosecution is prepared to proceed and is prepared to proceed very early in the new year. So dates that are set by the Chamber in the early new year will be quite satisfactory from our standpoint. A second point that I'd like to raise arises from a comment made by Your Honour on the 6th of May at the initial appearance -- or the further initial appearance where you indicated at page 20, line 20 to -- pardon me, 21 to 24, that the Chamber would be providing direction with respect to when the ten-day period for preliminary motions would start, and that was to take place after a decision had been -- or the decisions had been issued by the Chamber. Those decisions have now been issued, so I thought it might be useful for me to raise this question at this stage so that the Chamber might consider the matter further. That was the 6th of May, page 20, line 21 to 24. I have the extract which I can read to the Chamber if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: The relevant portion reads therefore -- this is after having recounted the nature of the proceedings and timing and so on. Your Honour said this: "Therefore, the Trial Chamber will determine the beginning of the ten-day period within which preliminary motions under Rule 72(A) are to be filed when it has decided upon the matters raised in the response of the Prosecutor." That has now been completed. There are a few further issues that I can outline unless the -- unless Your Honour wishes to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No, please proceed. Let me think about that while you proceed with the other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: As I mentioned, on the last Status Conference it will be my intention to file a bar table motion. That will be done in the first week of January. I simply wish to reiterate that as the plan. The purpose of the motion will be to ensure that the proceedings can proceed in a -- in an expeditious way. It's a trial management motion that will be made, hopefully, that will assist everyone in the courtroom. As well, it is my plan to file unless -- unless I receive a direction to the contrary, a pre-trial brief. In my experience in contempt cases, in some instances the Chamber has waived the necessity for filing a pre-trial brief; in other cases it was felt desirable. So I'm in the Chamber's hand on that. If I receive no direction one way or the other, it would be my intention to file a short one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I would think that that would be of assistance in this case, Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I will. The next point is --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say something about this before Mr. MacFarlane passes on to the next topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the pre-trial brief, the practice of the Tribunal, as well as the Rules -- Rules on Procedure and Evidence, show that a pre-trial brief is mandatory for the Prosecution but optional for the Defence. The Defence cannot be made to file a pre-trial brief, whereas the Prosecution has to. The last contempt trial launched against me was irregular, among other things, because the OTP did not file a pre-trial brief, although they were obliged to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, in this case Mr. MacFarlane has said he plans to file one, so any issue that you may have had in that regard has been resolved. Yes, Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: A brief matter which may or may not be relevant but I thought I should put it on the record in the event that it does become relevant in the future and that has to do with timing of the trial and timing of any future Status Conferences that might be directed. I have assigned this matter my highest priority so that I will be available, as I said before, at any stage in the early new year, which would encompass the first several months, so that I will be available and ready to go. I just wished the Chamber to note that from the 4th of April until the 20th of May, I will be quite a distance from northern Europe and will not be able to return then. So if either the trial is set during that period or there's a Status Conference that arises during that period, with the greatest of respect it would be very difficult for me to attend then. I just wished -- it may well be moot. It might not arise at all, but I thought I should note that for the record so that the Chamber is aware of that reality for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. MacFarlane. At the risk of going out on a limb, which 30-plus years of experience around the courts has cautioned me against, I would -- it seems to me unlikely that another 120 days would elapse, thereby necessitating a further Status Conference before a trial date is set. To be more definite than that it would be imprudent for me to be, but I -- but we've noted the -- your period of unavailability.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That was my only purpose in raising it. A further issue which is probably more in the nature of placing matters on the record so that it's clear, and again this might be moot, it might be unnecessary, but on reviewing the proceedings in this case and in the previous contempt case that the accused just referred to, it's become apparent to me that where motions are filed by the accused, they are often perhaps invariably greatly oversized, and that creates a delay in the proceedings. It creates a delay when it comes to translation, and it becomes very difficult for the other party to respond where no previous authority was sought, so to file an oversized motion or filing. So my request at this point is simply to ask the Chamber to remind the accused that where an oversized filing is anticipated, that brief authority from the Chamber is required from the Rules, and I would content myself with that should Your Honour think that that reminder or that direction is appropriate in the circumstances. I do that in the context of the desire to have this matter proceed expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Seselj, in terms of Mr. MacFarlane's last comment, without repeating everything that he would have said, I would draw what he has said to your attention and that you would conduct yourself accordingly. I don't know if you have any comments on that before I ask Mr. MacFarlane to move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Hall, you did not take part in the previous contempt proceedings against me, and therefore you're not steeped in the matter, but Mr. MacFarlane, who did participate, simply doesn't know what he's talking about today. I didn't file any motion then, especially not an extensive one, but this time I will file a motion only under Rule 65 ter, which motion will encompass five pages, but it will have over 100 pages of annexes. You know that under Rule 65 ter there are no limitations. In the proceedings against me, the OTP has filed 6.000 documents with several hundred thousand pages. Even strategy textbooks of the Command Staff Academy in Belgrade, then the brigade rules, corps rules, and so on. This time I will not file any other motion, and last year I didn't even file a motion under Rule 65 ter, because I thought I didn't need to call witnesses. Now I changed my mind, and the material that I will submit nobody has the power to limit. There are no limitations in the Rules nor in the instructions as to the length of the motions. The motion itself will have five pages, whereas the annexes may have as many as 200 pages. I didn't have time to count -- to count the pages. That is why, for reasons of fairness, I put it out that the Registry should check which portion of that material has already been translated, and much has. When it goes -- when it comes to newspaper clips that show that protected witnesses made public appearances and made public their name, their number, their code-name, and everything else, that material is extremely relevant. And if the Registry goes about its job conscientiously, then much time and resources of the Tribunal will -- will be saved. However, if they do translate everything again from scratch, then I can't help it. But obviously Mr. MacFarlane doesn't know what he's talking about. During the last proceedings, I find -- I filed no motions, except for the initial one where I informed the Trial Chamber that I would represent myself and who would be my assistant and my Case Manager. As far as I remember, there weren't any more motions at all. And if Mr. MacFarlane should be aware of any extensive motion of mine from the last but one proceedings, then I dare him to put that to me, but I stay by my words that he obviously doesn't know what's talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. MacFarlane, is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Might I respond to that issue, Your Honour, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I suspect Mr. Seselj has quite a number of matters on his mind and perhaps his memory is failing him on this particular point. On the 19th of March of this year, Mr. Seselj filed an oversized brief before the Appeals Chamber in the previous contempt proceedings, and on the 9th of April, the Appeals Chamber found that: "Seselj's repeated filings of oversized submissions without prior permission constitute unacceptable interference in the timely and efficient functioning of the Tribunal." And in that same decision the Appeals Chamber issued a warning to the then accused of the consequences of oversized filings. The Appeals Chamber said this: "It warns Seselj that should he persist in submitting oversized filings without prior permission, the Appeals Chamber reserves the right to disregard arguments set out in the excess portion of any oversized submission without allowing him the opportunity to refile or otherwise comment on the submission." That's a matter of public record in the decisions from the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: There is one further --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have something more to say. You see, Mr. Hall, either Mr. MacFarlane is a man of very modest intellectual capacity, or he lacks elementary ethics. In the previous contempt proceedings, he said that I filed oversized motions, and then I put the facts to him showing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I am not going to pursue this particular issue any further. I've heard what you have said. I've heard Mr. MacFarlane in reply. I'm moving on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But mind you, I cannot leave this unanswered. As far as Mr. MacFarlane is concerned, my correspondence with the Appeals Chamber, that is irrelevant for these proceedings. Let us wait for the appeals proceedings and there will be other rules in force. I'm not burdening the first instance proceedings, and I didn't do so the first time around. But Mr. MacFarlane is making up things, and now he's run out of arguments, and now he's saying that I filed oversized briefs to the Appeals Chamber. But in the main proceedings, I had motions that are longer than 1.000 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, the -- Mr. MacFarlane had first merely, as I understood it, reminded you through the Chamber of the Rules in terms of filing oversized briefs, and in his reply to your response of that, he cited the Appeals Chamber's decision in a matter involving yourself. We are not here today concerned with whether, as a fact in these contempt proceedings, you have so far or that you intend to file oversized brief. It was merely a reminder as to what the Rules are and the limitations imposed by the Rules. So there is no issue to be resolved and therefore there is no point in you pursuing this matter further. Yes, Mr. MacFarlane, your next point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Mr. Hall, I informed you that it is my intention to file but one motion, which is a 65 ter motion with evidence. The preliminary statements of witnesses and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: With annexes. Yes, we heard -- we heard that. It's on the record. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The next and I believe final issue I'd like to raise is a matter of in part substance and in part procedure and does not directly involve the accused but I thought I should raise it, and that involves my colleague to the right, Ms. Lori Ann Wanlin. I will be seeking a limited right of audience from the Chamber at the forthcoming trial, and I would like to lay the foundation for that request. Ms. Wanlin was first appointed to assist me in early 2008 in respect of another matter, and since then she has assisted me on a number of matters and her role has continually increased as these matters have progressed through this Tribunal. Ms. Wanlin was called to the bar in Canada in spring of this year, so that is a new development which I believe is relevant, but there's five factors that I would ask the Chamber to consider in assessing my request. The first is the one I just mentioned, that Ms. Wanlin is now called to the bar and is a member of a Canadian Bar. Secondly, in terms of her ability to deal with matters arising in the Chamber, Ms. Wanlin is fluently bilingual in both of the working languages, and I can only say that I envy that, but she is able to -- she is perfectly fluent in both French and English. Thirdly, I can say that as a result of my observations of Ms. Wanlin over the past three years, her ethical standards are of the highest order and certainly meet the high expectations of the Office of the Prosecutor, although we are not a member of OTP, but her ethical standards are extremely high. Fourthly, Ms. Wanlin has been appointed by the Registrar on five separate occasions, three as assistant to me as amicus curiae Prosecutor, and two separate matters as assistant to me as amicus curiae investigator. Ms. Wanlin participated in all five of those appointments actively and in an intensive way to the point where she is extremely familiar with the practice and procedure on the Rules and the evidence in the Tribunal and has made a point of understanding relevant portions of international law to a level that I think is a model for a current legal assistant. Of interest as well, as a result of the decision of the Chamber on the 2nd of December, 2010, one of the issues that may well and probably will arise relates to the notion of publication through electronic means, and in particular, through the internet. Ms. Wanlin worked for the better part of a year at the Canadian Internet Policy and Public Interest Clinic housed at the University of Ottawa and has a very good if not rare understanding of that very difficult intersection between the law and the internet so that it's my respectful submission that she will be able to provide assistance to the Chamber, which I can only, once again, envy. There are several previous precedents that I am aware of on my review of the judicial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before I go on, I smiled at your last comment because I have just seen, and I emphasise "seen," not yet read, with interest two articles on the Ontario Bar Association web site about this intersection between the law and the internet, which I have shared with my colleagues back in the Bahamas, which I would have received as an associate member of the OBA, and I'm glad that some of us understand what it's about, because I confess that it may be an age thing that it's an area which is terra incognito to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that it's not an area of expertise for me either and perhaps it is an age issue. I understand that the intersection between the internet and the law has recently been argued before the Supreme Court of Canada as well, so it's a fast-moving area, and with Ms. Wanlin's background and expertise, it struck me that she could be of service to the Chamber on that issue. As I mentioned on my review of the jurisprudence, there are several previous precedents that would lay a further foundation for this type of direction or order, and if Your Honour or if the Chamber thinks it appropriate, it might be a wise avenue to arrange for consultation with the Registrar on -- on those other precedents, although Your Honour might conclude that that's not necessary, but that is an avenue that might be available. My proposal at the end of the day is that the Chamber grant Ms. Wanlin a limited right of audience in this particular case, it being confined to contempt of court -- contempt of the Tribunal matters and that she be allowed to actively participate in the presentation of evidence, cross-examination of evidence, and the presentation of argument, all of which would be under my direct supervision and direction. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, of course, I claim no expertise in the rules relating to rights of audience before this Tribunal, but we have noted your foundation application in the course of these proceedings, and the appropriate ruling would be delivered in due course. Thank you. Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a reply to that. I absolutely disagree with the request just formulated by Mr. MacFarlane. First of all, only he was appointed as amicus curiae, and only he can appear in that role. There were no two amicus curiae appointed with a right of audience. Mr. MacFarlane could bring in his wife, his son, his daughter, his neighbour, and ask that they also be granted right of audience. How he's going to choose his associates is his own business. The Registry has certain rules about how that can be done and I have nothing against that. I ask that I be appointed assistants as well. But not every clerk from his technical team should be given the right of audience. I know Mr. MacFarlane, and I have experience in working with him, and I'm sure that no proper ethical standards can be applied in his work and that of his associate. I will ask people from my defence to check what personal relationship exists between Mr. MacFarlane and Ms. Wanlin. How come he chose precisely her. If there are going to be two amicus curiae in this courtroom, why should all of them -- both of them be Canadian. Why wouldn't one of them be from Bangladesh? Why should I be forced to listen to Canadians. In the main trial against me the OTP had ten counsel. Some of them left. Some of them were about to depart, and I'm still here. So if this right of audience is granted, if this person is appointed, I will keep reiterating that it is inappropriate and inadmissible. She cannot cross-examine witnesses because she is not amicus curiae. Secondly, the fact that she is an alleged expert for a new field of law that is linked to internet is really a fascinating fact. However, in that case, Mr. MacFarlane should ask the Trial Chamber that she come here as an expert witness so that she can come and testify about this field if that is necessary, and then I should be able to cross-examine her, including examining her past, her family ties, her ties to Mr. MacFarlane, and things like that. It will be -- it would be very interesting to hear that in the courtroom. And to have her appear as a double of Mr. MacFarlane here in the courtroom, no, the conditions for that have not been met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seselj, there may be merit in some of what you have said, but I need only remind you of my initial response to Mr. MacFarlane's request, which was that I have -- I claim no expertise on the matter of rights of audience before the Tribunal, and that having heard the foundations of his submission, which -- foundation may not have been the precise word he used, but what I understood him to be saying is that what he has said today is the background to a formal application which will be made and a decision will be rendered in due course. So there is no disadvantage to you one way or another. Is there anything else, Mr. MacFarlane?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Normally I wouldn't find it necessary to make this comment, but some aspects of the accused's comments I found quite offensive vis-a-vis Ms. Wanlin. I simply wish to note for the record that at the beginning, when Ms. Wanlin was first appointed, she was specifically recommended to me by the Associate Dean of the Faculty of Law at the University of Manitoba, and that is how I first met with Ms. Wanlin. I interviewed her, found her to be excellent, and that's simply, quite simply, the background. She was highly recommended to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. It's always unfortunate when persons use the opportunity of being in a court to make personal offensive comments of that nature. Yes. Is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: No, thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have something with respect to that, Mr. Hall. See here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, I will hear you when Mr. MacFarlane is finished. Yes, Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No, I appreciate the opportunity to make the preliminary comments. I have no further comments at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. What do you wish to add, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to add this: International criminal law is quite a young field of law. It is not based on extensive jurisprudence. The jurisprudence produced by this Tribunal and by the Rwanda Tribunal is criticised by some of the most eminent lawyers in the world. All serious law schools in the world. The most influential ones have excellent experts for international criminal law who produced a large number of papers questioning the very existence of The Hague Tribunal. And imagine now here when you have an amicus curiae appearing as a prosecutor telling you that he received a recommendation from the Dean of the law school of -- from Manitoba. It's been 34 years since I graduated from the school of law. It's been 31 years since I acquired my Ph.D. in law, and I have never, ever heard that the law school of Manitoba is known in the world because of some of their eminent professors, and I didn't hear of anybody from Europe travelling for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, there is no point in us going any further down that road.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- further studies to Manitoba.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we conclude today's proceedings, are there any concerns about your health or the conditions of your incarceration which you wish to raise with the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane, I promised that I would return to this matter of the -- when the -- how the ten-day period would run before we adjourn. It's something which I would prefer to give further thought to, and the Chamber will give the necessary direction having -- having considered the matter that you would have reminded me is still a live issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- I would remind the accused that in contempt proceedings, the preliminary motions under Rule 72(A) are to be filed within a 10-day period once he has received all the supporting material in accordance with Rule 66. And no party having any other matter to raise, we would adjourn these proceedings, and I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: at 3.49 p.m.
